title: Going global: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and America — go there first to get big
dek: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's the opposite — you go there first to get big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.
why: Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas investment experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers, especially the second half on AI transforming organizations and pricing, which is the densest.
who: Founders building or preparing overseas brands, cross-border e-commerce operators, and early investors watching consumer going global.
skip: The opening small talk and 15th anniversary congratulations, about 1 minute, can be skipped.

points.h: The old cross-border big-seller path is a dead end
points.body: Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border big seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-type mindset, with dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. A decade ago these companies made money faster than other paths from a profit perspective, and many investors liked them. But distribution-type companies are essentially traffic-type companies: the more stores, the more likely to get traffic. When platform goods aren't abundant, distribution isn't opposed; once goods are abundant, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, three red lines: goods not matching descriptions harms consumers, brushing orders harms other merchants, and putting small cards for private domains harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel places great importance on consumer experience, and these behaviors hit that protective wall head-on.

Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce; all of life is about choices being more important than effort. He gives four choices: region choice, channel choice, product category choice, brand positioning choice. On region choice, he has always advocated seizing the European and American markets first, because of strong paying power, high internet penetration, and more importantly, the brand can build momentum. This isn't their invention; when Japanese and Korean brands went global, they all seized Europe and America. On category choice, they change their advice every three years: the earliest three years supported products common to China and abroad, where domestic supply chains didn't need modification to sell overseas, like Anker's power banks which were almost identical except for voltage; the second three years advised overseas-specific products, because Chinese supply chains all went overseas, and common products had no differentiation; the most recent three years is product 3.0: electrified, with chips, with algorithms.

points.h: It's not that you go to Europe and America after getting big; you get big by going there
points.body: Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and America when I'm big’, and he says it's exactly the opposite: you go to Europe and America to get big. He gives the example of Cupshe, a swimwear company: a couple, with $50,000 of goods, and their first stop was the US. $50,000 is sales goods, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. He recently looked at AI smart hardware, starting from Kickstarter crowdfunding with a thousand or ten thousand products, even pre-collecting payment before ordering, with no capital, which is also a good way to test the waters. He even advises big companies entering the European and American markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce in; both big and small companies should first do the four singles well: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

points.h: After AI, good companies don't just find demand, they create it
points.body: Wei Zhe says with AI, excellent companies don't look for demand; they should lead demand and create demand. He gives the example of a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally not electrified, they electrified it, with chips and algorithms; the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, and the map of the universe's movements is regular. He, not originally an astronomy enthusiast, would buy one, click at home in Silicon Valley, and it automatically aligns with Orion for you, tells you the best effect is at 3 a.m., you press it and go to sleep, and the next day it takes the photo for you. This lets everyone become a good astronomy enthusiast. Another example is a cross-border class student doing curtains; after electrification, they didn't sell well in the US because American electricians are expensive, so he put solar panels on the window, turning electric curtains that need electrician installation into DIY ones; originally always one or two hundred million, now four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

points.h: In the AI era, still using subscription fees means you're behind
points.body: Wei Zhe says in the AI era, if you still have the subscription fee mindset, you're behind again; they all advise companies to do back-end charging, software charging, called tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest way, a bit like advertising charging by time instead of usage. This time AI brings out the most ideal charging model in all human education: pay according to your usage of AI software, services, or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, a monthly subscription wastes two weeks. They suggest that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not the old SaaS monthly $9.9 subscription model. An AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, no charge if you don't read; smart cycling trainers are the same, after recharging, one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

points.h: Adding AI is more promising than AI plus
points.body: Wei Zhe has a viewpoint called AI plus or plus AI; he reverses the phrase and is more optimistic about plus AI rather than today's AI plus. The difference is: plus AI is hardware humans have already accepted, and you AI-ify it; rather than creating a previously unseen hardware because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept a brand new hardware. For example, Oura makes rings because you first accepted rings; some make you hang a camera under your neck, which I find harder, I haven't accepted that hardware. So they are very optimistic about adding AI to already accepted hardware. They invested in a capacitive stylus that is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad, it doesn't add an extra pen for you, it just AI-ifies your pen. He also particularly wants to transform a top-two overseas fitness equipment company, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with AI-generated ones, you want a male, it's male, you want a black person, it's black, install two cameras and AI can guide fitness.

points.h: Channels aren't flat; they're a pyramid
points.body: Wei Zhe says channels aren't multiple channels multiple paths, each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and which channel to launch new products in first. What is a light goods channel, what is the main waist volume channel, the pyramid design differs for different categories and brands. He gives Anker: making power bank mecha seems a bit low, to enter the consumer electronics high ground Soundcore earphones you have to enter Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot doesn't matter, but it can rebrand the brand, Apple is the pyramid top. Pop Mart must open on London Oxford Street, even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose, but it must be propped up there. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light goods channel, when Amazon delists you, you dump there, you can't sell on Amazon and here too, consumers are confused.

Wei Zhe says he really dislikes spending heavily on marketing. Many Chinese brands going overseas or cross-border e-commerce are willing to add 2% of revenue to marketing expenses, but consumers don't get it. He says, do you dare to add 2% of revenue to R&D expenses? He has met many bosses with 1 billion or 2 billion scale; a 1 billion boss says 20 million for R&D, I don't know what for. He says see, there's the problem, you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing makes the platform happy, consumers don't get it; but 2% thrown at R&D, consumers get it. He always firmly believes good products speak for themselves, marketing is just, your R&D is 1, marketing is 0, if you have a good thing you can amplify it, if you don't have that 1, never put many 0s. He gives three judgment signals: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and you crush it by doubling performance; second, you sell at the same price as it; third, you sell online, and offline channels come to you.

points.h: AI doesn't just change products, it transforms every position
points.body: Wei Zhe says AI has two important things for enterprises, big, medium, and small all must do well: first, the combination of products with AI, second, how the organization changes through AI. He sees cross-border e-commerce companies as almost the industry among all he has seen that most should use AI to transform every position. Every position asks what AI can do for you: product selection, content generation, ad placement choices, essentially all algorithms; previously relying on human experience, experience is definitely not as powerful as algorithm iteration. Customer service AI-ified, no customer service, customer service is just you training your customer service agent; ad placement you train an agent; product selection, product display, product image and video generation all AI-ified. He says this is the first and only industry he has seen where the entire company organizational chain can be transformed by AI. He also says they most oppose placing many people overseas, with or without AI, called no unnecessary overseas staffing.

points.h: Not just let AI work, but let it participate in decisions
points.body: Wei Zhe explains AI and organization very simply; many companies have P series and M series, P is professional, M is Management. Many people are used to letting AI do P, doing the work, generating images which was originally a P series job. But truly great companies don't just let AI do P series work; you gradually let it do Manager, Director, VP work. He gives a real case of AI pricing: the company originally wanted to sell at 35 euros, AI said you can sell at 55, the company really went to 55, really sold, volume similar to before at 35, but earned 20 euros more. He says AI has no courage, it's bolder than you, it has compared everything across the web for you. He also says even if AI has hallucinations, with so many large models in the world, China and the US, they won't dream the same dream at the same time, so you must cross-validate.

terms.def: Wei Zhe's term for a charging model based on AI usage, replacing monthly subscriptions.
Wei Zhe's coined term: dare to define a price and not lower it; when peers catch up to the same performance, you compete on performance.
Single market, single category, single channel, single brand; Wei Zhe advises overseas companies to focus first.
Wei Zhe's overseas category advice: from non-electric to electric, electric with chips, chips with AI algorithms.

quotes.text: Price-performance ratio means my performance and quality are the same, you do the same as me, I compete on price. Price-performance ratio is what I dare to define; after I set it, I don't lower the price; if a peer catches up to the same performance, I increase performance.

You say a non-electric product gets copied by others in a month. Electric? You have many European and American access requirements, you'll lead by about six months. OK, your chip can add another twelve months. OK, your algorithm might lead for a lifetime.
